Students applying for admission into ABM must do so through the URI Graduate School admission system.
Applicants must have earned at least 75 credits before they are eligible to apply.
Students will be enrolled in ABM after they have met all Graduate School admission requirements, and completed 90 undergraduate credits.
ABM students will be separately coded to distinguish them from other graduate students.
K. 1.1 Credit Requirements.
Only students accepted into the ABM program will be able to double count credits towards both the bachelor’s and master’s degrees.
The total number of credits that will be allowed to be double counted is up to one-third of the total credits required in the master’s program.
Only 500-level courses and 400-level courses designated for graduate credit are eligible to be double counted.
K. 1.2 Credits Taken Outside of a program or from another department.
Students can transfer credits between URI programs and departments.

Only credits earned at URI may be counted toward the master’s portion of the ABM.
K. 1.3 Time-to-degree Limit.
Students must complete all graduate degree requirements for an ABM within 2 years after their enrollment and coding as ABM students.
An additional year for programs with more than 30 credits may be allowed with the permission of the Graduate School.
Failure to complete the ABM in the allotted time effectively ends the ABM and students will not be able to double count credits.
K. 1.4 Program of Study.
ABM students must complete a Program of Study and submit it to the Graduate School in their first semester of enrollment in the graduate program.
The Program of Study lists the courses to be taken to fulfill the requirement of the master’s degree and those carried over from the undergraduate career.
If any changes in the original Program of Study are made, a new Program of Study must be submitted as soon as possible.
All ABM programs will have an established list of core courses and suitable electives that can be used to satisfy the requirements for the combined degree.
K. 1.5 Nomination for Graduation.

A Nomination for Graduation form must be submitted to the Graduate School by the ABM Program Coordinator in a student’s final semester.
Deadlines for submission are published in the Deadline Calendar on the Graduate School website.
The master’s degree will not be conferred on students prior to completion of their bachelor’s degree.
Simultaneous conferral of both degrees may be considered.
K. 1.6 Grades and Grade Point Averages.
Students must meet the acceptable grade requirements as described in Section 10 of the Graduate School Manual.
K. 1.7 Continuous Enrollment.
Continuous enrollment (see Section 4.40 of the Graduate School Manual) is required once students are coded and enrolled as ABM students.
K. 2.0 ABM Program Coordinators.
Every ABM shall have at least one Coordinator.
The Coordinator must assure that students enrolled in ABM are advised by the Coordinator or designated participating faculty.
Coordinators recommend approval or denial of applicant admissions to the Graduate School, approve Programs of Study, and submit Nominations for Graduation.

Coordinators and participating faculty also respond to programmatic questions from potential applicants, maintain files on active students, and keep records of the number of students who have participated in the ABM Program from its inception.

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The field of Health Outcomes seeks to identify and measure the relationship between medical treatments and the outcomes achieved in real-world environments. It is applied to help understand what works and what doesn’t work in health care. As a subspecialty, the field of Medication Outcomes endeavors to determine the consequences of prescription drug therapies, including a medication's effectiveness, safety in general use, and its economic impacts on patients and the health system. Contributing disciplines include epidemiology, health economics, statistics, humanistic outcomes assessment and health policy.

2 As healthcare organizations are increasingly challenged to deliver more effective and efficient care, professionals with expertise evaluating health outcomes will have key roles addressing this challenge.
Because medication is a fundamental aspect of contemporary medical care, skills in medication outcomes assessment are needed to ensure that policies and protocols for using prescription drugs are guided by robust evidence, informed by sound methodologic analyses and based on valid interpretations of scientific and statistical data.
There exists a growing demand for professionals who possess these skills, which are typically not emphasized in clinical training programs.
The URI College of Pharmacy offers a full -time MS/PhD program, with a track specializing in Health Outcomes research.
Yet it is not possible for many working professionals to enroll in a full-time graduate program delivered on campus.
The online graduate certificate program will provide a more feasible option to obtain these skills.
Our market survey revealed a high degree of interest in the program among health care professionals.

Interest was particularly strong among pharmacists, who view additional training in health outcomes to benefit their career advancement.
Graduates from URI's nationally renowned Doctor of Pharmacy program have strong brand loyalty and rapport with faculty that can be leveraged to recruit students would favor URI over competitors.
Our graduate certificate program will be specifically focused in Medication Outcomes, providing differentiation from competing certificate programs that provide training in Health Outcomes.
It will be delivered online and comprise 12 credits.
It will be administered as four 3-credit courses delivered sequentially, to be completed within a 9-month period spanning September - May.
All courses will emphasize application, with case and project-oriented activities.
The first course will provide an introduction to medication outcomes evaluation, covering basic principles for conceptualizing medication outcomes, and methodologic and statistical approaches for collecting and analyzing data.

The second and third courses will teach student techniques for conducting pharmacoepidemiologic and pharmacoeconomic evaluations and interpreting and applying evidence in these fields.
The fourth course will extend the skills covered in the prior courses, covering advanced topics and guiding the student through the steps of conducting a chosen medication outcomes project that is relevant to the student's work role and/or interest.
Students completing this certificate program will be able to 1.) Develop and structure a medication outcomes evaluation; 2.) Collect and analyze data using contemporary methods from the fields of pharmacoepidemiology and pharmacoeconomics; and 3.) Translate results of medication outcomes studies to healthcare decision-makers to optimize prescription medication use in the varied work environments.
The online Graduate Certificate in Medication Outcomes meets the Provost's academic priority for active e-learning via technology-enhanced pedagogy and online programs.
Further, it aligns with key goals of URI's Academic Strategic Plan.

One goal of this Plan is to enhance student success by equipping learners with skills that are in demand in an ever-changing world, which this proposed certificate program aims to achieve.
The Medication Outcomes certificate program also addresses this goal's strategy of facilitating the implementation of new learning pedagogies and the expansion of modes of course delivery and assessment by leveraging space and time in new ways.
This

3 program also addresses the Plan's goal for diversity and social justice, as the Certificate program curriculum will include strategies for reducing racial disparities in medication use, and for optimizing the use of pharmacy resources in programs that serve vulnerable populations. Additionally, this certificate program will augment knowledge in health and sciences, and develop the workforce to enhance public safety, as described in the Plan's goal to expand research, scholarship, and creative work. What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
Prescription medications are a top publi c policy concern, and are increasingly impacting the viability of organizations that deliver and finance health care.

Retail prescription drug expenditure comprises approximately 10% of US national health expenditure.
Many new pharmaceutical innovations have annual prices exceeding six figures, arguably justified by ever-increasing costs of research and development.
To ensure that expensive medications are used judiciously, decision-makers require outcomes data specific to their population to design policies to guide how medications should be used to maximize their benefits in a cost-effective manner.
The US does not set drug coverage policy at the federal level.
Even in Medicare, policy for determining which medications are covered is determined by each private Part D drug benefit sponsor (subject to broad federal guidelines).
Outside of Medicare. policies for medication use are crafted by hospitals, state Medicaid programs, commercial insurers, pharmacy benefit managers, medical group practices, health centers, among other entities.
In each of these settings, personnel with specialized skills are required to evaluate current evidence and generate local data to determine the actual health outcomes experienced by patients.
Medication Outcomes evaluation provides these skills.

We conducted a needs assessment survey in spring 2021 to ascertain the demand for graduate certificate-level training in Medication Outcomes evaluation.
The results validated the need for this program.
We solicited survey participants using the RI Department of Health’s publicly available email list of licensed pharmacists.
Additionally, we recruited participation through personal requests to contacts at Care

5 New England, Coastal Medical, Lifespan, RI Medicaid, and the RI Department of Health.
Colleagues from the College of Pharmacy shared the survey link with their contacts, and the survey was also posted on LinkedIn.
There were 114 respondents, among which there were 109 who indicated that the program would have value to themselves or coworkers.
The responses of these 109 participants were analyzed.
Forty percent of respondents were age 25-34 (44/109), while roughly 20% were age 35- 44 years, and 8.3% were under the age of 25, suggesting interest in the program following graduation.
Over 30% of respondents were age 45 or older.
These results indicate interest in the program across age groups.
The majority of respondents (77%) were pharmacists.
Other disciplines represented included MBA (9.2%), MPH (4.6%), Medical Doctor (2.8%), and having a master’s degree in another field (e.g.
MD Ed, MHA).
The most frequent work settings of respondents were hospital (n = 20), community pharmacy (n = 18), primary care (n = 14), pharmaceutical industry (n = 11), and the health insurance industry (n = 8).
